title: Russell's Paradox and the Birth of Type Theory (1901-1908)
explainer: In 1901 Bertrand Russell found that an unrestricted notion of 'the set of all sets that do not contain themselves' makes formal logic contradict itself. To block the paradox he developed a theory of types, sketched in 1903 and given mature form in his 1908 paper, which stratifies objects into levels so a thing can never be a member of itself. Every statically typed language you compare in this lesson, from Java's class hierarchy to Haskell's kinds, descends from this fix: a type system is, at bottom, a discipline for keeping a program from asking a self-referential question it cannot answer.

title: Robin Milner, Algorithm W, and the Origin of Type Inference (1978)
explainer: Robin Milner's 1978 paper 'A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming' introduced Algorithm W, a method that infers a program's most general type with no annotations at all, and proved that a well-typed program under it 'cannot go wrong.' He built it for the ML language, and the same mechanism, now called Hindley-Milner after J. Roger Hindley's related 1969 proof, still drives type inference in OCaml, Haskell, F#, Rust, and Swift. When you compare how much type annotation each language demands versus infers, you're really comparing how much of Algorithm W's power each one inherited.
